Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.abstract: CUPID is a next-generation tonne-scale cryogenic experiment that will search for the neutrinoless double beta decay $(0νββ)$ of $^{100}$Mo. It will be located at the Gran Sasso National Laboratory (Italy) and will employ the cryogenic calorimetric technique to reconstruct the energy deposited in Li$_{2}$MoO$_{4}$ crystals, in which the isotope of interest is embedded. Preliminary measurements have been performed with the CUPID VSTT (Vertical Slice Test Tower), a prototype tower designed to test the detectors' response and the apparatus' mechanical and thermal stability. In addition, a key objective was to demonstrate the improved performance of germanium-based cryogenic light detectors. In CUPID, light detection is used for both particle identification and pile-up rejection. Li$_{2}$MoO$_{4}$ is a scintillating crystal, enabling particle identification by exploiting the dependence of light yield on particle type. This requires collecting the Li$_{2}$MoO$_{4}$ scintillation light, peaking at $\sim$600 nm, with a $\sim$300 $μ$m-thick high-purity germanium wafer placed next to the crystal. The wafer is also equipped with concentric Al electrodes biased at a few tens of volts. This bias improves the signal-to-noise ratio by an order of magnitude thanks to the Neganov-Trofimov-Luke effect. This work presents preliminary results on the performance of the VSTT light detectors and of its Optical Injection System.

Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.title: Adaptive carrier signal synthesis for frequency-division multiplexed cryogenic detector readout
Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.authors: Timo Muscheid, Benedikt Keppner, Daniel Crovo, Robert Gartmann, Marvin Fuchs, Lukas Scheller, Oliver Sander, Luis E. Ardila-Perez
Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.abstract: Frequency-domain multiplexing is a fundamental technology for readout of cryogenic detector arrays on a single transmission line. Synthesizing a large number of static carrier tones for resonator stimulation eventually drives the cryogenic low-noise amplifier beyond its P1dB, introducing detector signal distortion. Scaling array sizes to O(10^6) detector pixels therefore demands minimizing the total power on the transmission line by continuous tracking of the resonances, which requires the readout electronics to be capable of updating the carrier tones dynamically. This work presents an scalable FPGA-based implementation for carrier signal synthesis based on a numerically controlled oscillator and a polyphase filter bank, enabling real-time frequency adaptivity as well as frequency resolution of 4 mHz to precisely tune the operating point, while simultaneously reducing resource usage compared to the current memory-based implementation.

Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.title: Development of a Cryogenic Anti-Coincidence System Based on Scintillating Crystals Read Out with Kinetic Inductance Detectors for BULLKID-DM
Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.authors: T. Lari, G. Spina, A. Acevedo-Rentería, L. E. Ardila-Perez, L. Bandiera, C. Bonomo, M. Calvo, M. Cappelli, R. Caravita, F. Carillo, F. Cescato, U. Chowdhury, D. A. Crovo, A. Cruciani, A. D'Addabbo, M. del Gallo Roccagiovine, M. De Lucia, G. Del Castello, D. Delicato, F. Ferraro, M. Folcarelli, S. Fu, R. Gartmann, M. Grassi, V. Guidi, D. L. Helis, L. Malagutti, A. Mazzolari, A. Monfardini, T. Muscheid, D. Nicolò, F. Paolucci, D. Pasciuto, L. Pesce, C. Puglia, D. Quaranta, C. M. A. Roda, S. Roddaro, M. Romagnoni, G. Signorelli, F. Simon, A. Tartari, E. Vázquez-Jáuregui, K. Zhao, M. Vignati
Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.abstract: The BULLKID-DM experiment has been proposed to search for WIMP-like dark matter particles with a mass of 1 GeV or lower and with a WIMP-nucleon interaction cross section down to $10^{-43}$ cm$^2$. To achieve this goal, the experiment utilizes a detector consisting of a stack of 16 silicon wafers instrumented with phonon-mediated superconducting Kinetic Inductance Detectors (KIDs), to be operated at the underground facility of the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso (LNGS), Italy. To reduce the residual background arising from $γ$-rays, neutrons, and muons, a cryogenic active anti-coincidence system (veto) operating at mK temperature, surrounding the main detector, is under development. The veto detector consists of segmented scintillating crystals read out by phonon-mediated KID light detectors. Current status and future developments of the veto system are presented. In particular, we focus on cryogenic tests of both bismuth germanate (BGO) and gadolinium aluminum gallium garnet (GAGG) crystals, which had been previously chosen as veto candidate crystals according to our preliminary studies on the dependence of their optical properties (i.e. light yield and scintillation decay time) on temperature. We finally present the operation and preliminary tests of a two-module veto prototype with multiplexed readout.

Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.title: Quantized resistance limitations for graphene p-n junction devices
Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.authors: Tamar M. Padwa, DaVonne Henry, Dominick S. Scaletta, Heather M. Hill, Antonio L. Levy, Dean G. Jarrett, David B. Newell, Albert F. Rigosi
Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.abstract: Developing high-resistance quantized Hall resistance standards requires accessing values beyond the robust value seen in epitaxial graphene (R_{\mathrm{H}}=\ \frac{1}{2}\frac{h}{e^{2}}). This study evaluates the available parameter space of the coefficient of effective resistance across various epitaxial graphene p-n junction topologies, including rectangular, Corbino, and triangular layouts. Because mapping desired resistances to device configurations is mathematically degenerate, an automated Landauer-Büttiker Python solver was developed for all three topologies and was validated by cryogenic multi-terminal transport measurements and LTspice simulations. By analyzing the Shannon entropy of available states, it is found that rectangular checkerboards maximize topological complexity and tunable outputs, whereas Corbino geometries exhibit highly constrained resistance availabilities.

Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.title: Towards Cryogenic AI Hardware: Over 99% Precision In-Memory Computing at 4 K with 3-bit Ferroelectric Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 Capacitors
Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.authors: Ella Paasio, Simon Thomann, Rikhard Ranta, Ruhan Kartik, Sozaraj Rasappa, Andrea Padovani, Hussam Amrouch, Sayani Majumdar
Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.abstract: High-accuracy cryogenic hyperdimensional computing (HDC) is demonstrated using Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 (HZO) ferroelectric capacitors (FeCAPs) as multilevel analog memories for capacitive compute in-memory (CIM) architectures. On the ISOLET spoken-word dataset, FeCAP-stored vectors achieve up to 92% classification accuracy at 4 K, while charge-domain matrix-vector multiplication (MVM) exhibits near-ideal behaviour with linearity of 1 and error probability below 1% for 4x4 and 4x8 configurations, operating below 3 V. Unlike the performance at 300 K, HDC and CIM at 4 K remains resilient to electric-field-cycling-induced fatigue, thanks to enhanced cryogenic device characteristics, including reduced state variability, strongly suppressed leakage current and stable retention, as well as 78% faster switching. Furthermore, these multibit FeCAPs exhibit endurance beyond 1E9 cycles with polarization degradation below 8%, preserving multilevel integrity. Benefits can also be observed at 300 K, following cooldown and wake-up pulsing at 4 K and subsequent warming up. These results establish multibit FeCAPs as a highly reliable, ultra-low-energy, and accurate analog CIM platform for future cryogenic AI-computing hardware.

Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.title: Accessing Electrode Edges: Upright Mounting for Site-Specific Cryogenic Atom Probe Tomography of Lithium-Ion Batteries
Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.authors: Syeda Ramin Jannat, James O. Douglas, Neil Mulcahy, Lukas Worch, Aigerim Omirkhan, Zhenyu Guo, Yuanzhu Zhao, Maria-Magdalena Titirici, Ifan E. L. Stephens, Mary P. Ryan, Baptiste Gault, Michele Shelly Conroy
Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.abstract: Cryogenic atom probe tomography (cryo-APT) is increasingly being used to map the three-dimensional distribution of highly reactive species in heterogeneous materials, including those found in battery systems. However, site-specific preparation of localised features and liquid-solid interfaces remains challenging, particularly when regions of interest (ROIs) are concentrated along electrode edges that are difficult to access using conventional mounting geometries. Here, we present a cryo-APT workflow incorporating an upright-mounting procedure that enables targeted specimen preparation of localised regions using plasma focused ion beam (PFIB) microscopy and milling under cryogenic conditions. We first demonstrate the approach using an electrolyte-wetted graphite electrode, successfully preparing and analysing a specimen containing both an edge-localised electrolyte deposit and the underlying graphite and Cu current collector. We then apply the workflow to a cycled graphite electrode, targeting Li dendrites concentrated around the electrode perimeter and successfully preparing and analysing the targeted Li-rich region. Beyond battery systems, this approach offers potential for site-specific cryo-APT of edge-localised features across a broader range of material systems, where conventional specimen preparation geometries may limit access to ROIs.

Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.title: Surrogate-Assisted Compact-Model Extraction for SKY130 CMOS at 77 K
Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.authors: Aaron Wang, Olivia Gzamouranis, Vaibhav Lohia, Hershel Fei Xun Weiner, Olivia Seidel, Richard Cavanaugh, Giuseppe Di Guglielmo, Nhan Tran, Davide Braga
Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.abstract: Cryogenic circuit design requires compact transistor models that reproduce measured low-temperature behavior and run in standard circuit simulators. We fit BSIM4 parameters to measured I-V curves of SkyWater 130 nm (SKY130) transistors at 77 K using a neural surrogate of NGSpice. The surrogate maps compact-model parameters and device geometry to the complete set of output and transfer characteristics. Extraction is a bounded least-squares search: a bank of NGSpice simulations supplies initial candidates, finite differences of the surrogate supply the local Jacobian, and NGSpice re-simulates the resulting cards before selection. On 18 measured geometries, we compare a search over seven card parameters with a search over 43 parameters selected by NGSpice sensitivity. Relative to NGSpice re-simulations of the previously released cards, the two searches reduce the in-sample mean relative root-mean-square error (RRMS) by 17% and 26%, respectively. The 43-parameter search has the lower overall error, but the seven-parameter search has the lower mean on high-bias curves, and some individual curves have higher error than with the released cards under both searches.

Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.title: Gateless 1T-DRAM for cryogenic memory applications
Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.authors: Seung-Bum Yim, Ki-Nam Park, Hyun-Jun Kang, Jun-Young Park, Sihyun Kim, Jaeyong Jeong, Joon-Kyu Han
Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.abstract: Cryogenic memory has emerged as a key technology for quantum-computing systems. In this Letter, a gateless one-transistor DRAM (1T-DRAM) operation is demonstrated at cryogenic temperatures. As the temperature decreases, the latch window expands from 0.26 V at 300 K to 2.26 V at 4 K, resulting in stable memory operation with a large sensing margin of 414 μA at 4 K. Suppressed Shockley–Read–Hall recombination at cryogenic temperatures improves static retention exceeding 500 s at 77 and 4 K, with dynamic retention exceeding 1000 s. These results demonstrate the potential of gateless 1T-DRAM for high-density cryogenic memory applications.

Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.title: Erratum: “Controlling the recovery time of the superconducting nanowire single-photon detector with a voltage-controlled cryogenic tunable resistor” [Appl. Phys. Lett. 127 , 212601 (2025)]
Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.authors: H. Wang, N. D. Orlov, N. Noordzij, T. Descamps, J. W. N. Los, V. Zwiller, I. Esmaeil Zadeh

Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.title: Graphene Transfer for Vertical Amorphous-Selenium Photodetectors: Fabrication, Optical Transmission and Operation at 77 K
Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.authors: I. Tzoka, M. Boukhicha, V. A. Chirayath, B. Brown, M. Rooks, M. Febbraro, S. Park, S. Abbaszadeh, K. Hellier, J. Asaadi, A. K. Rumaiz
Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.abstract: Graphene can serve as a VUV transparent electrode in vertical photodetector devices. Using an optically transparent graphene as a top-electrode of amorphous selenium (a-Se) photoconductor requires transfer process compatible with the thermal and chemical sensitivities of a-Se thin films. The baking and polymer-removal steps of conventional commercial Trivial Transfer graphene procedures are undesirable because heating can promote selenium crystallization and prolonged solvent exposure can cause delamination. We implement two alternatives: PMMA-free transfer of nominal 50-layer graphene and transfer of nominal 10-layer graphene using an approximately 80 nm PMMA support removed in acetone at 40C. Raman G and 2D bands identify graphene after transfer. Separate graphene/MgF2 specimens are characterized by dark-corrected transmission measurements over 120-325 nm and compared with earlier single-layer and nominal 6-8-layer Trivial Transfer spectra. The completed graphene/a-Se/Cr devices produce bias-dependent voltage transients under pulsed 415 nm illumination at 293 K and 77 K. These results establish an a-Se-compatible fabrication route for graphene-electrode devices and demonstrate vertical device operation at both room and cryogenic temperatures. The completed devices provide a platform for detection-efficiency studies, and direct VUV photoresponse measurements now underway.

Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.title: A Multiobjective Optimization Framework for Sensor Array Design in Magnetocardiography
Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.authors: Kesavaraja C, Sammita Kashyap, Korak Biswas, Pranab Dutta, Kushal Patel
Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.abstract: Magnetocardiography (MCG) noninvasively measures cardiac magnetic fields. Conventional cryogenic systems use fixed multichannel arrays, whereas room-temperature sensors enable flexible placement to reduce array size and measurement redundancy. The present study aims at developing a scheme to identify the optimal sensor placements by utilizing three methodological sensor optimization frameworks such as physics driven, experimental data driven and a hybrid combination of both. The physics-driven method optimizes continuous planar coordinates using D-optimality, spatial correlation, and leastsquares error. The data-driven method uses measured spatiotemporal fields and pole-geometry metrics, while the hybrid method integrates both approaches. The evaluation is performed using training objective, Pearson correlation, normalized root-meansquare error (NRMSE) and pole separation(mm), orientation(°) and trajectory(mm) errors, where physics-driven optimization identified 16 sensors with a correlation of 0.9914 and an NRMSE of 0.0139, with pole separation, orientation, and trajectory errors of 3.71 mm, 1.38°, and 3.55 mm, respectively. Data-driven optimization shows diminishing improvements beyond 17 sensors, achieving correlation 0.9840, NRMSE 0.0035, and pole errors of approximately 4.30 mm, 1.70°, and 6.80 mm. The hybrid method achieves correlation 0.9945 and NRMSE 0.0201 with 14 sensors, reducing sensor count by 12.5% relative to the physics-driven configuration. Its pole errors of 6.50 mm, 2.31°, and 7.50 mm satisfy the study-defined thresholds, balancing array compactness with magnetic-field morphology preservation. These results show that optimized placement helps alleviate the complexity of data redundancy and enhances the performance of MCG as a routine cost-effective clinical measurement.

Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.title: Optical characterization of microcellular PET and crystallized PEN reflectors in liquid argon for LEGEND-1000
Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.authors: Marta Babicz, Laura Baudis, Andreas Leonhardt, Francesco Piastra, Lorenzo Pietropaoli, Stefan Schönert, Gloria Senatore, Esteban Tapia Peñas, Tim van de Vendel
Cryogenic Measurements & Instrumentation.abstract: Efficient collection of liquid argon (LAr) scintillation light is essential for background rejection in the LEGEND experiment. We investigate microcellular polyethylene terephthalate (PET) and crystallized polyethylene naphthalate (PEN) as candidate reflector materials for LEGEND-1000. Their optical responses to 450 nm light and 128 nm LAr scintillation are measured in LAr and complemented by room-temperature reflectance measurements in air. Under scintillation illumination, PET coupled to a PEN foil and crystallized PEN increase the detected photoelectron yield by factors of $2.36\pm0.11$ and $1.75\pm0.10$, respectively, relative to a black-metal-velvet reference. A Geant4-based optical model yields reflectivity estimates at $450~\mathrm{nm}$ in LAr of $(90\pm4)\%$ for PET and $(81\pm5)\%$ for crystallized PEN, compared with $(80\pm5)\%$ for the Tetratex reference. These results motivate further investigation of both materials for LAr instrumentation, including their radiopurity, long-term cryogenic stability, and performance under matched detector conditions.

Scientific Instrumentation & Automation.title: A 40 Gbit/s FPGA-based RoCEv2 transport for detector readout: development and performance
Scientific Instrumentation & Automation.authors: Sheng Dong, Jingzhou Zhao, Haoxin Wang, Tingxuan Zeng, Fei Li
Scientific Instrumentation & Automation.abstract: Recording the complete input of a detector trigger allows trigger algorithms to be replayed and studied offline. For the BESIII main drift chamber (MDC), this requires moving tens of Gbit/s from trigger FPGAs into server memory without loss. Remote direct memory access over Converged Ethernet (RoCEv2) lets commercial network adapters write such data into host memory. Detector readout also needs record boundaries that the receiver can check, replay from a verified copy, and host buffers that are reused only after consumption. We present a 40 Gbit/s FPGA RoCEv2 transport that provides these functions. Records are aggregated into CRC32C-checked blocks, and unacknowledged data are kept in DDR memory and verified before replay. Acknowledgment-aware retention writes to DDR only the data that are not acknowledged in time. The transport runs on a ZCU102 board and on the 9U VME Trigger Core Board (TCB). With records of 128 B to 4 KiB it comes within 0.4% of the packetization limit of the link, delivering 36.9 Gbit/s of payload at a path MTU of 1024 B, and its block latency is set by the time needed to fill a block. On a direct link, acknowledgment-aware retention cuts DDR writes for large blocks from 106% to 0.03% of the payload, and injected DDR access errors stay within their queue pair. On the TCB, three 16.4 TB transfers through two switches lost at most five packets each, all recovered by replay. An installation at the MDC is under test.

Scientific Instrumentation & Automation.title: Telemetric calorimetry for wireless continuous reaction profiling
Scientific Instrumentation & Automation.authors: Sukwoo Lee, Evan A. Weingarten, Michael F. Reynolds, Kevin Sun, Alejandro J. Cortese, Huw M. L. Davies, Alyosha C. Molnar, Paul L. McEuen, Song Lin
Scientific Instrumentation & Automation.abstract: Real-time monitoring of chemical reactions is often achieved with specialized instrumentation along with custom-designed reactors or intrusive sampling. In this study, we introduce reaction telemetry, a wireless analytical strategy that enables remote, nonintrusive monitoring directly within operating reaction vessels. This approach uses light-powered microelectronic devices that communicate optically and function as autonomous sensing elements. We demonstrate continuous calorimetric measurements across diverse chemical reactions relevant to pharmaceutical and fine chemical synthesis, including photochemical and electrochemical systems, providing access to reaction kinetics under native operating conditions with subsecond temporal resolution. The resulting measurements will support catalyst evaluation, safety assessment, and mechanistic investigation and will accelerate data-driven reaction discovery. By embedding analytical functionality directly within reaction vessels, reaction telemetry establishes a general framework for information-rich observation of chemical processes across research, development, and education.

Scientific Instrumentation & Automation.title: SimpleClock: a satellite-disciplined oscillator for astronomical instrumentation
Scientific Instrumentation & Automation.authors: Albert Wai Kit Lau, Bruno Pollarolo, Juan Mena-Parra
Scientific Instrumentation & Automation.abstract: SimpleClock is a low-cost, high-stability timing reference designed for astronomical experiments that combines a global navigation satellite system (GNSS) timing receiver, a digitally tunable 10 MHz microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) oven-controlled oscillator, external thermal regulation and autonomous control. It provides 10 MHz and pulse-per-second references at an estimated prototype hardware cost of US\$500. Independently enabled frequency and phase feedback support precise point positioning (PPP) with Galileo's High Accuracy Service (HAS), satellite-based augmentation system (SBAS) solutions and standalone operation. Three-unit phase comparisons separate component noise and characterize disciplined-output stability over 200\,000 s recordings. Across five configurations, each analysed over 200\,000 s, equivalent single-unit differential Allan deviation and time deviation at 1000 s span $3.5\times10^{-13}$--$1.0\times10^{-12}$ and 115--447 ps, respectively. The maximum equivalent time deviation over averaging times from 1 to 50\,000 s spans 143--1090 ps. These results support applications in astronomical timing, including low-frequency very long baseline interferometry (VLBI).

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Data-driven reassessment of lattice matching in ScAlN/GaN heterostructures grown by sputter epitaxy and molecular beam epitaxy
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Atsushi Kobayashi, Takuya Maeda, Thai-Son Nguyen, Huili Grace Xing, Debdeep Jena, Yoshio Honda
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: We reassessed the lattice-matching behavior of ScAlN thin films grown on GaN by constructing a unified dataset from sputter epitaxy, molecular beam epitaxy (MBE), and literature reports. The dataset comprised 197 samples, including 32 MBE-grown and 70 sputter-grown films from our laboratories and 95 literature data points, for which Sc composition, growth temperature, film thickness, polarity, growth technique, and a- and c-axis lattice constants were compiled. The compiled data were analyzed using a neural-network-based surrogate model to extract smooth lattice-constant trends within the experimentally covered parameter range, and these trends were subsequently parameterized by empirical polynomial functions of Sc composition and growth temperature. The lattice-matched Sc composition of ScxAl1−xN to GaN was estimated to be x ≈ 0.10–0.13, which is lower than the conventional value of approximately 0.18 and is only weakly dependent on growth temperature and growth technique. In contrast, the c-axis lattice constant was strongly dependent on growth temperature and decreased at higher growth temperatures. This c-axis contraction, together with the reduced c/a ratio, is consistent with growth-temperature-dependent bond softening and local structural distortion in ScAlN, providing a possible structural link to polarization switching in ferroelectric nitrides.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Tunable coupling between valley and magnetic excitons in WS2/CrSBr heterostructures
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Jianchen Dang, Liza Godziashvili, Kaichen Xie, Arun Ramanathan, Vadym Kulichenko, Alejandro Busto, Jia-Yi Ji, Robert Boyd, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Sina Najmaei, Daniel Rhodes, Luis Balicas, Xavier Roy, Ting Cao, Xiao-Xiao Zhang
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: Interfacial coupling in van der Waals two-dimensional (2D) heterostructures offers an effective route to tailor the electronic, optical, and magnetic properties of materials. Versatile control and precise engineering of such interlayer interactions can be further achieved through external parameters, like electric field, magnetic field, optical excitation, as well as layer stacking geometries. Here, we examined the magneto-optical properties of 2D semiconductor heterostructures made of antiferromagnetic CrSBr and a monolayer WS2, both of which host intriguing excitonic properties. We identified a type-II band alignment between these two layers and the magnetic proximity effects from CrSBr, manifested by an enhanced Zeeman valley splitting in the WS2 layer. The interlayer charge transfer shows strong spin selectivity and is governed by the relative alignment between the valley-spin polarization of photoexcited carriers in WS2 and the magnetization in CrSBr, giving rise to spin-sensitive circularly polarized photoluminescence (PL) from WS2. Furthermore, the highly anisotropic electronic dispersion in CrSBr enables stacking-dependent control of interlayer interactions, as inferred from a twist-angle dependence of PL quenching. Our work establishes a highly tunable 2D system that integrates valleytronics and magnetic excitons through multiple coupling channels, opening up new opportunities in all-optical manipulation of spin and magnon states and for the development of flexible spin-optoelectronic devices.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Dislocation-templated antiferromagnetic domains in epitaxial NiO
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Alexandra Fonseca Montenegro, Justin Michel, Fengyuan Yang, Roberto C. Myers
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: Controlling antiferromagnetic (AFM) domains is essential for spintronics, yet predictable manipulation remains challenging due to their lack of net magnetization. Here, we utilize scanning electron microscopy electron channeling contrast imaging (ECCI) to observe the formation of nanoscale AFM domains in epitaxial NiO/MgO(001) at interface dislocations. Thermal cycling across the Néel temperature reveals that while domain contrast vanishes in the paramagnetic phase, the features re-emerge at identical spatial locations upon cooling. Diffraction-vector-dependent ECCI imaging, governed by a relative tilt contrast model, indicates that the domains stem from localized rhombohedral distortions of volumetric twin-type T-domains. These T-domains are stabilized by the long-range shear stress field of interface misfit dislocations (MDs). By tracking a film thickness series from 23 to 46 nm, we resolve a transition in oxide relaxation mechanics from primary 60° interface MDs along ⟨110⟩ to a cross-slipped network of pure edge 90° MDs deviated toward ⟨100⟩. We demonstrate that ECCI identifies the Burgers vector and line direction of these MDs via strict g→·(b→×u→) invisibility criteria, and an Eshelby interaction energy model accurately predicts the asymmetric nucleation of specific T-domains along MD flanks. Quantitative image analysis shows that T-domain volume fractions track the spatial configuration of the evolving MD networks, providing a framework for defect-engineering AFM textures using one-dimensional defects.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Kinetic arrest of a disordered first-order phase transition in strained V 2 O 3 thin films
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Sindhunil Barman Roy
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: We develop a continuum phenomenological theory for the kinetic arrest (KA) of a first-order phase transition, taking the thermal and electric field-driven metal–insulator transition in epitaxial V 2 O 3 thin films as a prototype. By defining a coarse-grained mesoscopic order parameter ϕ ( r , t ) ≡ 1 − θ ( r , t ) / θ 0 representing the metallic volume fraction coupled to the primary structural monoclinic distortion θ , we formulate a Time-Dependent Ginzburg–Landau framework integrated with a non-local elastic interaction kernel and an Imry–Wortis quenched disorder landscape. We derive an explicit dynamic criterion for the KA boundary T K ( E ) by analyzing the divergence of the intrinsic order-parameter relaxation time relative to experimental observation timescales. Our framework rigorously decouples the thermodynamic driving force from the kinetic activation barrier. We demonstrate that epitaxial substrate-induced clamping elevates local elastic barriers, pinning domain boundaries and stabilizing an arrested, inhomogeneous mosaic of metallic and insulating phases down to cryogenic temperatures. The simulated transformation kinetics exhibit an Avrami exponent suppression to values n < 1 , reflecting slow, hindered domain-wall propagation. Furthermore, we examine the effect of an external electric field as an isothermal mechanism that lowers this kinetic barrier, providing a phenomenological description of threshold de-arrest and multi-level resistance states. We critically discuss this electronic barrier-lowering mechanism in comparison with electrothermal Joule heating, establish diagnostic criteria to distinguish them, and contextualize these non-equilibrium dynamics with related phenomena in disordered superconducting films.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Universal unidirectional magnetoresistance in magnetic heterostructures
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Qian Chen, Junwen Sun, Qingjie Guo, Tieyang Zhao, Zhaocong Huang, Jingsheng Chen, Ke Xia, Ya Zhai, Xiangrong Wang
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: Unidirectional magnetoresistance (UMR) is a widely observed nonlinear transport phenomenon in magnetic heterostructures, yet a unified symmetry-based description of its angular response remains experimentally unresolved. Here, we demonstrate that the angular response of UMR in magnetic heterostructures can be quantitatively captured by a two-vector magnetoresistance (MR) framework. Namely, MR depends on magnetization and an effective interfacial electric field. The UMR amplitude scales linearly with current and decreases with increasing magnetic-layer thickness, consistent with an interfacial origin. In ultrathin heterostructures, higher-order angular harmonics emerge and become more pronounced in Co/Ti than in Ni/Ti, which does not support a systematic trend expected for a dominant orbital Hall contribution. More importantly, the observed angular responses are fully described by the two-vector framework without invoking a specific spin–orbit-mediated conversion mechanism. These results establish the applicability of the two-vector MR framework to nonlinear magnetotransport and provide a general symmetry-based description of UMR across a broader class of magnetic heterostructures.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Nitrogen Defect Coupling in Epitaxial LaFeO3 From Structural Reconstruction to Water Oxidation
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Le Wang, Shan Lin, Min-Ju Choi, Krishna P. Koirala, Mark E. Bowden, Jeffrey A. Dhas, Zihua Zhu, George E. Sterbinsky, Tiffany C. Kaspar, Chongmin Wang, Scott A. Chambers, Ho Nyung Lee, Peter V. Sushko, Yingge Du
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: Earth-abundant ABO3-type perovskite oxides provide a versatile platform for understanding how anion chemistry and defects govern electrocatalytic behavior. Here, we use epitaxial LaFeO3-xNy thin films to reveal how dilute N incorporation (<0.8% N/O) couples to defect formation, structural reconstruction, and water oxidation. Nitrogen-plasma-assisted pulsed laser deposition introduces N and is accompanied by reduced oxygen content, localized Fe-metal exsolution, and pronounced lattice expansion, while preserving predominantly Fe3+ in the bulk of the film. Ab initio calculations identify a plausible charge-balanced extended defect configuration involving coupled oxygen and Fe vacancies with substitutional N incorporation, reproducing the experimentally observed lattice expansion while preserving the bulk-average Fe oxidation state. The resulting electronic-state redistribution is accompanied by substantially modified electrical transport and nearly two orders of magnitude higher initial oxygen evolution reaction (OER) activity than undoped LaFeO3. Under OER conditions, however, the highly active as-grown state is metastable: near-surface N depletion and Fe0 oxidation/removal accompany rapid initial activity decay toward a quasi-steady state. pH-dependent kinetics and post-OER anion redistribution are consistent with possible lattice-oxygen participation. These results establish relationships among dilute anion incorporation, coupled defect reconstruction, electronic properties, and electrochemical behavior in perovskite oxides.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Ab initio study of magnetic interaction in R NiO 2 : Role of rare-earth size and epitaxial strain
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Ramasamy Murugesan, Shiyu Deng, Marie-Bernadette Lepetit

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Influence of interfacial roughness amplitude and periodicity on giant chiral asymmetry of domain wall mobility in epitaxial Cu/Pd/Co/Pd(111) films
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: N. N. Chernousov, A. S. Pashenko, A. G. Kozlov, A. A. Turpak, A. S. Samardak, A. V. Davydenko
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: We investigate the influence of interfacial roughness amplitude and lateral periodicity on the chirality-dependent mobility of domain walls (DWs) in epitaxial Si(111)/Cu(2-7 nm)/Pd(3 nm)/Co(0.7 nm)/Pd(3 nm) heterostructures. By varying the Cu buffer layer thickness, we systematically modify the morphology of the magnetic interfaces while maintaining a constant composition and thickness of the Pd/Co/Pd trilayer. Scanning tunneling microscopy reveals that increasing the Cu thickness leads to the development of a hierarchical interfacial morphology characterized by increasing roughness amplitude and lateral periodicity. We observe a dramatic enhancement of the asymmetry between the velocities of DWs with opposite chirality in the creep regime, reaching a velocity ratio of approximately 50000 in the sample with a 7-nm-thick Cu buffer layer. This value exceeds by more than an order of magnitude the effective saturated asymmetry previously observed in Pd/Co/Pd structures with roughness controlled by the bottom Pd layer thickness. Despite comparable root-mean-square interface roughness in both series, the Cu-buffer-induced morphology exhibits a substantially larger characteristic lateral periodicity. We propose that the enhanced asymmetry originates from the different spatial organization of interfacial disorder, which modifies the pinning energy landscape and amplifies chirality-dependent thermally activated DW propagation. Our results suggest that engineering not only the amplitude but also the lateral spatial correlations of interfacial roughness provides an effective approach for controlling chiral DW dynamics in magnetic heterostructures.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Strain Controlled Hydrogen Interstitial Site Preference and Hydride Phase Suppression in Epitaxial Vanadium
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Xin Xiao
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: Understanding hydrogen behavior in transition metals is crucial for energy storage and sensing technologies. Here we combine density functional theory (DFT) calculations with in-situ electrical measurements to reveal how epitaxial strain governs hydrogen interstitial site selection and phase stability in vanadium. Our calculations demonstrate a robust thermodynamic preference for tetrahedral (T) over octahedral (O) sites, with the energy difference modulated by lattice anisotropy through strain-tunable H 1s-V 3d orbital hybridization. Experimentally, epitaxial V films on MgO(001) exhibit a critical thickness-dependent crossover: 50 nm films show characteristic first-order alpha-beta hydride transitions, while 10 nm films display continuous solid-solution behavior with complete transition suppression. This crossover is governed by the progressive relaxation of epitaxial strain with increasing film thickness: the 10 nm films retain strong coherent strain that flattens the free-energy landscape and suppresses hydride nucleation, whereas the 50 nm films approach the strain-relaxed bulk limit where long-range elastic interactions restore first-order phase behavior. Finite-size truncation of elastic fields and interfacial electronic reconstruction further reinforce this dimensional crossover. Our work establishes a unified framework connecting atomic-scale orbital physics to mesoscopic phase thermodynamics, providing design principles for strain-engineered metal-hydride systems.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Engineering antiferromagnetic (LaVO3)m/(PrVO3)n superlattices
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: A. Benedit-Cardenas, G. Masset, M. Bugnet, M. Martirosyan, G. Steciuk, S. Migot, J. Ghanbaja, L. Pasquier, K. Dumesnil, Q. M. Ramasse, O. Copie
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: In this study, we demonstrate the atomic-scale engineering of antiferromagnetic (LaVO3)m/(PrVO3)n superlattices grown by MBE on (001)-oriented SrTiO3 substrates. Our work achieved a precise layer-by-layer control, revealing how interface-driven structural distortions can be systematically tuned. X-ray diffraction and reciprocal space mapping confirm both the epitaxial strain state and the high crystalline quality of the superlattices. High-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy further uncovers layer-resolved atomic displacements, where La3+ and Pr3+ exhibit antipolar motions modulated by the superlattice periodicity. The alternate stackings of LaVO3 and PrVO3 yield a unique antiferromagnetic transition temperature, which can be tuned by adjusting their relative proportions. This behavior exists despite the distinct spin ordering temperatures observed in the constituent materials. Layer-resolved spectroscopic measurements reveal that the hybridization of La and Pr 5d orbitals with O 2p orbitals is also modulated and directly correlated to the oxygen octahedra rotations. By determining the orbital hybridization and mapping the cation displacements as proxies, we can visualize indirectly the trilinear coupling between oxygen octahedra rotations and antipolar rare earth displacements. Notably, the interfacial oxygen octahedra connectivity between cubic SrTiO3 substrate and orthorhombic vanadate layers significantly influences the structural distortions. These distortions, almost quenched near the interface, relax over few unit cells, demonstrating how strain and interfacial effects propagate through the superlattice. This study illustrates how artificial superlattices can be engineered to control structural distortions at the atomic scale, offering a pathway to tune the magnetic properties through strain-distortion relationships in perovskite oxides.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Epitaxial integration of GaN $μ$-platelets and thin films on metallic TiN using a hybrid approach
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Philipp M. John, Thomas Auzelle, Pierre-Marie Coulon, Blandine Alloing, Ileana Florea, Mikel Gómez Ruiz, Jonas Lähnemann, Lutz Geelhaar, Oliver Brandt
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: We demonstrate the synthesis of epitaxial, self-organized GaN $μ$-platelets on metallic TiN thin films. To this end, we first nucleate self-assembled GaN nanowires with number densities between 0.01 to 300 $μm^{-2}$ by molecular beam epitaxy. Subsequent overgrowth of these seed nanowires by metal-organic vapor phase epitaxy yields GaN $μ$-platelets with corresponding number densities. The platelets exhibit N-polarity and form an ohmic contact to the metallic TiN substrate. By adjusting the growth conditions during the metal-organic vapor phase epitaxy, particularly the carrier gas and precursor ratio, the morphology of the GaN can be controlled across a broad range. Growth under N$_{2}$ carrier gas and with a 1:1 NH$_{3}$/trimethylgallium precursor flow ratio results in platelet ensembles with broad diameter and height distributions. In contrast, employing an N$_{2}$/H$_{2}$ carrier gas mixture promotes the formation of more homogeneous ensembles with narrower size distributions around a diameter of $\approx$2 $μm$. Finally, N-rich growth conditions under H$_{2}$ carrier gas enhance lateral growth, leading to the formation of coalesced GaN layers. GaN grown under these latter conditions exhibits strong near-band-edge emission, accompanied by only weak deep-level luminescence at room temperature.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Strain-induced spin reorientation transition and associated anomalies of magnetization dynamics in epitaxial Y 3 Fe 5 O 12 films
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Nikolay A. Pertsev

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Pseudomorphic SiGe/GeSn superlattices grown by molecular beam epitaxy on Ge(100)
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Allison M. McMinn, Tyler T. McCarthy, Hryhorii Stanchu, Xiaoyang Liu, Alexander Golden, Martha R. McCartney, David J. Smith, Shui-Qing Yu, Yong-Hang Zhang
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: SiGe/GeSn superlattices with total thicknesses of ∼0.5 μm were grown directly on Ge(100) substrates by molecular beam epitaxy, achieving Sn incorporations up to 11.4% while maintaining pseudomorphic growth. High-resolution x-ray diffraction exhibits well-defined superlattice satellite peaks and distinct Pendellösung fringes in close agreement with simulations, indicating precise control of layer thickness and composition. Reciprocal space mapping shows no detectable in-plane lattice relaxation within experimental resolution, consistent with pseudomorphic growth, and transmission electron microscopy confirms uniform superlattice periodicity, with high-quality growth and very low defect densities. Together, these results indicate that this superlattice architecture can enhance Sn incorporation while suppressing strain relaxation. This behavior is consistent with partial strain compensation between the SiGe and GeSn layers, which mitigates the effects of lattice mismatch and the limited equilibrium solubility of Sn. These results establish SiGe/GeSn superlattices as a viable CMOS-compatible platform for group-IV heterostructure electronics with enhanced Sn incorporation and precise compositional and structural control. Such control enables advanced band structure engineering and provides a promising foundation for concepts such as momentum (k)-space carrier separation for infrared photodetectors.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Intrinsic-interfacial dipole coupling and band alignment in a 2D polar MoSi2N4/MoSiGeN4 van der Waals heterostructure
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Pan Zhao, Wenxuan Wang, Yu Liu, Qimeng Li, Mi He, Xiangcao Li, Xiao Tian, Facheng Jin, Zhen-Yi Jiang
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: Polarization-dependent electrostatics provides an effective route to regulate band alignment in two-dimensional (2D) polar van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures, yet the roles of intrinsic and interfacial dipoles remain unclear. Here, using first-principles calculations, we reveal an intrinsic-interfacial dipole coupling mechanism in the MoSi2N4/MoSiGeN4 heterostructure. Despite weak net interlayer charge transfer, pronounced interfacial charge redistribution produces distinct dipolar responses in the two opposite polarization configurations. The dipole contributions partially cancel in UP configuration but reinforce each other in DOWN configuration, giving 2D polarizations of 5.70 and 6.16 pC m−1, respectively. This electrostatic modulation reduces the bandgap from 1.93 to 1.49 eV, while preserving type-II alignment and strongly shifting the band edge positions. The DOWN configuration satisfies the thermodynamic requirements for overall water splitting, whereas the UP configuration is unfavorable for hydrogen evolution. DOWN also exhibits strong optical absorption and a corrected solar-to-hydrogen efficiency of 19.58%. These results identify intrinsic-interfacial dipole coupling as a key mechanism governing polarization-controlled band alignment in 2D polar vdW heterostructures.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Out-of-plane interference effects in the angle-resolved photoemission of epitaxial graphene
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: E. Favorite, P. Krüger, Ph. Rosenzweig, R. Joshi, S. Williams, B. Matta, K. Küster, M. Hashimoto, U. Starke, H. Nakamura
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: The epitaxial growth of monolayer graphene by Si sublimation of 6H-SiC(0001) is one of the most effective ways of producing large-scale monocrystalline graphene samples of high quality. However, graphene is left interacting with a reconstructed carbon buffer layer known as zerolayer graphene (ZLG) and the SiC substrate underneath. Beyond the mere creation of Dirac cone replicas, the effect of this interaction on photoemission measurements is poorly understood. We utilized synchrotron radiation for photon-energy-dependent angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) to investigate the complex final-state interactions of photoelectrons within the heterostructure of monolayer graphene, ZLG, and SiC. We identify multiple resonances in the photoemission intensity of the Dirac cone as a function of photon energy that originate from interlayer interference, confirmed with a multiple scattering model. We also demonstrate for the first time that the relative intensity of the replica bands induced by the $(6\sqrt{3} \times 6\sqrt{3})\text{R}30^\circ$ reconstruction scales with the electron kinetic energy. Finally, we resolved four nondispersing electronic states, which originate from the ZLG. Our findings show that the three-dimensional (3D) structure of SiC and ZLG manifests itself in the photoemission from two-dimensional (2D) epitaxial graphene. By revealing how 3D substrate architecture dictates the photoemission of a 2D layer, this work establishes a crucial framework for investigating the electronic structure of complex heterostructures via ARPES.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Modeling strained Cd 3 As 2 thin films and their behavior in magnetic fields
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: M. Smith, A. A. Burkov, P. P. Orth, I. Martin, Victor L. Quito

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Depth-resolved magnetization dynamics in Fe thin films after ultrafast laser excitation
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Valentin Chardonnet, Marcel Hennes, Romain Jarrier, Renaud Delaunay, Nicolas Jaouen, Marion Kuhlmann, Cyril Leveillé, Clemens von Korff Schmising, Daniel Schick, Kelvin Yao, Xuan Liu, Gheorghe S. Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Solvent/Antisolvent-Driven Etching of 2D Layered Halide Perovskite Microcrystals toward Endo-Epitaxial Heterostructures
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: Ajeet Singh, Sudhir Kumar Saini, Hriday Kumar Pal, Cara Elisabeth Bradsher, Sirous Khabbaz Abkenar, Roman Krahne, Liberato Manna
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: Engineering internal interfaces within single crystals remains challenging, particularly in soft ionic materials such as layered halide perovskites (LHPs), for which conventional lithographic approaches are difficult to implement. Here we report a solvent/antisolvent-driven strategy for controlled etching of LHP microcrystals, producing well-defined rectangular cavities. Etching initiates at the top surface and proceeds preferentially along the crystallographic [100] and [010] directions. Cavity dimensions are tuned through etching time, temperature and etchant composition. The reaction can be interrupted and resumed, enabling stepwise cavity evolution through successive etching cycles. The resulting cavities serve as confined templates for regrowth of compositionally distinct LHPs, yielding endo-epitaxial heterostructures with designed internal architectures. The approach extends across diverse LHP compositions and antisolvent systems, while sequential precursor addition controls the extent of internal regrowth. This strategy establishes a route to engineering internal heterointerfaces in single-crystal perovskites through controlled chemical etching and confined growth.

Thin Films & Interface Characterization.title: Shubnikov–de Haas characterization of superconductor–semiconductor heterostructures
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.authors: A. M. Zimmerman, Saeed Fallahi, Sergei Gronin, Tyler Lindemann, Patrick Sohr, Ray Kallaher, Alejandro Alcaraz Ramirez, Georg W. Winkler, Samuel M. L. Teicher, William Cole, Sebastian Heedt, Eoin O'Farrell, Gijs de Lange, Roman Lutchyn, Michael J. Manfra, John Watson
Thin Films & Interface Characterization.abstract: Hybrid superconductor–semiconductor nanostructures are a central component for research spanning condensed matter physics and quantum information processing. Continued progress relies critically on the ability to characterize, control, and optimize several intrinsic material properties, including spin–orbit coupling, band offsets, and disorder, in a device-relevant stack that necessarily couples the electronic states of a superconducting metal film and a semiconductor. Here, we report a new method to extract fundamental material parameters utilizing simple Shubnikov–de Haas oscillation measurements in heterostructures in which metallic electronic states are coupled to a two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) residing in an InAs quantum well beneath an aluminum thin film. Proper analysis of the full magnetoresistance data facilitates extraction of the quantum well carrier density, spin–orbit coupling strength, and both transport and quantum scattering times. Most importantly, the extracted scattering times in the 2DEG are impacted by the metal–semiconductor coupling strength, allowing us to quickly measure an upper bound for superconductor–semiconductor coupling without any fabrication or mK measurements. The wealth of information that is accessed with these simple measurements positions this methodology as an important tool for hybrid materials optimization.

Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.title: Bayesian inference with a polymer probabilistic computer
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.authors: Travis Wanless, Yuriy Bandera, Lubomir Kostal, Stephen H. Foulger
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.abstract: Bayesian inference weighs competing explanations of noisy data by sampling from a posterior distribution, a task that deterministic hardware performs only by simulating randomness. Probabilistic bits (p-bits) supply this randomness physically, but the few hardware networks of p-bits built so far use inorganic devices, address optimization or learning, and are judged without reference to the spread expected from finite sampling. Here we report a probabilistic computer built from solution-processed conjugated-polymer memristors. Four polymer p-bits, tracked online for drift and coupled in a closed Gibbs-sampling loop, sample competing, degenerate and cooperative posteriors over sixteen states with statistics that fall within the range of ideal p-bits, both in their distribution and in their autocorrelation, without any parameter fitted to the target. This agreement extends to new simulated sensor readings whose outcome was predicted before each run, including readings that point away from the true answer. Reprogrammed in software, the same circuit and controller reproduces the invertible AND gate of earlier p-bit networks, with its temperature fixed in advance rather than fitted. Polymer p-bits thus open a route to printed, large-area probabilistic computers that infer alongside their sensors.

Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.title: Sobolev theory for the inverse problem of time-dependent density functional theory on the torus
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.authors: Asbjørn Bækgaard Lauritsen, Mathieu Lewin, Jakob Oldenburg
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.abstract: We show that, given a sufficiently regular time-dependent density, there exists a unique potential such that the Schrödinger equation with this external potential has the prescribed one-particle density. We treat densities that are twice differentiable in time and of finite Sobolev regularity in space; the resulting potentials are continuous in time and of finite Sobolev regularity in space. Our method of proof is to rewrite the problem as a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a loss of derivatives, which we in turn handle with a completion-of-the-square argument. This is a refinement of our recent work [Lauritsen, Lewin, and Oldenburg, arXiv:2609.08984], which handled this loss of derivatives using the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem and treated analytic-in-space densities and potentials.

Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.title: quantEM: Quantitative Electron Microscopy Analysis from Differentiable Physics to Neural Priors
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.authors: Colin Ophus, Arthur RC McCray, Georgios Varnavides, Stephanie M Ribet
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.abstract: Quantitative electron microscopy includes imaging, diffraction, spectroscopy, and tomography measurements, and the analysis of these measurements increasingly requires solving inverse problems with physical forward models. Open-source software has made many of these analyses widely available, but most packages are organized around a single modality, so that multimodal analyses require moving data between packages, and new methods cannot easily reuse the physical models and optimizers of existing ones. Here we present quantEM, an open-source Python package for quantitative electron microscopy that uses PyTorch tensors for computation and automatic differentiation, and Zarr for storage. We implement each analysis method by writing a differentiable forward model and choosing a representation, loss function, constraints, and optimizer from a library of components, so that every method runs on CPUs and GPUs, can be saved and resumed, and uses the same calibrated data structures and visualization tools. We describe the current modules, including orientation and strain mapping, direct and iterative ptychography, tomography with neural representations, and X-ray and electron energy-loss spectroscopy, and show how we assemble combined methods such as ptychographic tomography from existing components. quantEM is available under the MIT license, together with documentation, tutorials, and curated example datasets.

Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.title: Real-axis least-squares bath discretization for real-time transport in quantum-dot Josephson junctions
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.authors: Ruixin Zhou, Bing Dong, Yiyan Wang

Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.title: sdos: spectral densities of large sparse Hermitian and generalized eigenproblems
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.abstract: sdos is an open Python package that computes the density of states (DOS) and related spectral quantities of very large sparse Hermitian matrices A, and of generalized problems A psi = lambda B psi, from Chebyshev moments estimated with random vectors. The density is reconstructed by the kernel polynomial method (KPM, the default) or by maximum entropy (Maxent); the same interface gives band energies, Fermi levels, local and projected densities, harmonic thermodynamics, exact HOMO-LUMO gaps and eigenpairs in a spectral window. Interfaces cover electronic (empirical tight-binding, DFTB, SIESTA) and vibrational (matrix-free LAMMPS Hessians) problems. I checked most ingredients against dense diagonalization or an independent code; the exceptions are listed in Sec. V. On a workstation (4 threads, 19 GB) the DOS of an 884,736-atom amorphous silicon model (a 6^3 tiling of a 4096-atom cell; 3.5 million orbitals; the orthogonal empirical tight-binding model of Kwon et al.) takes 71 s (M=100, R=2, no exact moments; 383 s with the default exact moments), and a matrix-free 2,097,152-atom crystal 10 min in 1.8 GB. A 17^3 replica of a 216-atom amorphous cell (1,061,208 atoms) agrees with exact Bloch spectra: electronic DOS in 229 s, matrix-free ACE vibrational DOS in 2.2 h on one GPU. Shift-invert, incomplete-Cholesky setup, exact moments of high order and Maxent at high moment counts do not scale. The underlying methods are due to Silver, Roder, Kress, Voter, Drabold, Sankey and collaborators; the Introduction states what is added.

Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.title: Active Fourier spectroscopy: From fixed sampling protocols to adaptive measurement
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.authors: J. Schröder, S. Howard, C. Eberle, J. Esslinger, N. Leopold-Kerschbaumer, K. V. Kepesidis, A. Döpp
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.abstract: Fourier-transform spectroscopy (FTS) is based on the Nyquist-Shannon theorem, which dictates a strict sampling protocol for the measurement of continuous signals. Here, we introduce active Fourier spectroscopy (AFS), a generalization of FTS in which measurements are still taken in the Fourier-conjugate delay domain, but where the most informative acquisition points are selected adaptively and the spectrum is reconstructed by sequential, uncertainty-aware inference rather than by fixed-grid Fourier inversion. Our approach relies on a theoretical insight that the Nyquist condition applies only under complete ignorance about the system under investigation, and shows how to systematically improve upon it when prior knowledge exists. AFS recovers conventional FTS when the prior is uninformative and falls back to it when prior knowledge is not supported by the data. We demonstrate AFS for optical spectroscopy in three settings vital to research and medicine: clinical FTIR (Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy)-based blood plasma analysis, optical metrology of structured laser beams, and hyperspectral imaging with an RGB camera. In each case, AFS reaches a higher target reconstruction quality from far fewer acquisitions and provides complete uncertainty quantification in real time, propagated rigorously through downstream analysis.

Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.title: Virtual-element pixelation for elevation-response recovery in linear-array three-dimensional photoacoustic imaging
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.authors: Shijie Li, Shengxian Li, Lin Huang, Jun Peng, Yuting Huang, Fang Wang, Yongqi Fan, Haifeng Liang
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.abstract: Mechanically scanned linear arrays provide a practical route to three-dimensional photoacoustic imaging, but a finite elevation response causes the same target region to contribute to several neighboring B-scans. A smaller scan step therefore increases sampling density without, by itself, removing elevation-direction mixing. Here, fine-step scans are formulated as overlapping observations governed by an experimentally measured post-beamforming elevation response. A 0.05 mm wire was used to identify a 15-point response for a 128-element, 20 MHz array scanned at 0.1 mm increments; this response was embedded in an extended-grid forward operator, and the resulting non-negative composite-regularized inverse problem was solved using the alternating direction method of multipliers. In an independent 0.08 mm crossed-wire experiment, the median elevation full widths at half maximum for delay-and-sum (DAS), Wiener, Richardson–Lucy, and ADMM reconstructions were 0.854, 0.665, 0.630, and 0.590 mm, respectively. ADMM achieved a median paired FWHM reduction of 26.3% relative to DAS, with a Peak SNR of 23.30 dB and a PSLR of −8.66 dB. Finger-vessel imaging showed reduced apparent broadening and structural merging. These results show that explicitly modeling experimentally identified inter-scan coupling can improve elevation localization using information already present in conventional fine-step scans without changing the transducer aperture.

Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.title: MyoGen: unified biophysical modeling of human neuromotor activity and resulting signals
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.authors: Raul C. Sîmpetru, Ricardo G. Molinari, Devon R. Rohlf, Rebeka L. Batichotti, Renato N. Watanabe, Leonardo A. Elias, Alessandro Del Vecchio
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.abstract: Understanding human motor control requires integrating cortical and spinal activity, muscle mechanics, and electrophysiology, which are typically studied in isolation. We present MyoGen, an open-source framework that unifies spinal circuitry, proprioceptive feedback, musculotendon dynamics, and multimodal electromyography generation. Using data-driven optimization benchmarked against human motor unit recordings, MyoGen produces motor unit population activity matching experimental discharge-rate distributions and variability across muscles. The framework generates decomposable surface and intramuscular electromyography, reproduces beta-band modulation of descending drive and its transformation into force, and implements key sensorimotor loop components. Dimensionality reduction of simulated agonist-antagonist electromyography reveals low-dimensional control manifolds consistent with recordings from able-bodied individuals and those with spinal cord injury. Here, we show that MyoGen provides a physiologically grounded simulation substrate, enabling systematic investigation of motor control principles, benchmarking of signal-processing algorithms, and exploration of experimentally inaccessible sensorimotor interactions.

Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.title: Quantum Cooling by Classical Shadows
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.abstract: Cooling to ground states of many-body Hamiltonians by imaginary-time evolution is central to quantum simulation, but its non-unitary aspect prevents direct implementation on a quantum computer. Existing routes restore it by importing structure from outside the intrinsic quantum dynamics, e.g. by parameter estimation on many copies or recursive compilation. Here, we show that a single randomized snapshot of the quantum many-body system is sufficient to steer the state along the cooling direction on average. Our algorithm, shadow chain, uses randomized measurements to collapse the state to its classical record, which fixes the next unitary update. Snapshots across steps form a trajectory that is a quantum-executable sample of an auxiliary-field path integral; fluctuations among trajectories are exponentially suppressed in system size. With the randomness supplied intrinsically by the Born measurement rule, the trajectories sample themselves rather than going through external accept-reject steps. The resulting algorithm is ansatz-free and exact upon extrapolation to the continuous limit, with the exponential cost confined only to system size rather than temperature.

Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.title: Quantum metrological advantage of high-order squeezed states
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.authors: Rubén Gordillo-Hachuel, Erik Torrontegui, Cristina de Dios, Ricardo Puebla
Scientific Modeling & Data Analysis.abstract: Quantum correlations can be harnessed to improve the precision in parameter estimation beyond classical capabilities. Under a standard interferometric or rotation protocol, it is well established that the optimal single-mode Gaussian state is a standard squeezed vacuum, which enables Heisenberg-limited precision. In this work, we investigate the potential metrological advantage of two distinct families involving high-order squeezing, namely, m th -phase and multisqueezed states. Our results show that these non-Gaussian states can grant a significant metrological advantage with respect to the optimal squeezed vacuum under equivalent conditions, i.e., at equal occupations. Their advantage holds at both low and large occupations, but its behavior critically depends on the chosen family of high-order squeezing. While higher squeezing orders enhance the advantage, this comes at the cost of higher-order observables in the measurement for full metrological performance. Finally, we study their robustness to standard decoherence channels, i.e., pure dephasing and zero-temperature damping. Employing standard squeezing as reference state, our results indicate a reasonable robustness against damping up to a certain noise strength, while their metrological advantage becomes fragile under pure dephasing. Our work shows the potential enhancement in quantum metrology beyond Gaussian states, carefully detailing the main challenges and limitations.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Hyperkagome antiferromagnetism in the iron garnet Almandine Fe$_3$Al$_2$Si$_3$O$_{12}$
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Minnong Zhang, Harald O. Jeschke, Daniel Guterding
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: Antiferromagnets on the hyperkagome lattice provide a three-dimensional route to strong magnetic frustration, but experimentally accessible realizations with well-established microscopic Hamiltonians remain scarce. Garnets are a broad family of materials in which magnetic ions can form two interpenetrating hyperkagome lattices, giving rise to spin glass, spin-liquid and hidden-order physics. Here we identify the iron aluminosilicate garnet almandine, Fe$_3$Al$_2$Si$_3$O$_{12}$, as a spin-$2$ hyperkagome antiferromagnet. Using density functional theory energy mapping, we determine a Heisenberg Hamiltonian for the high-spin Fe$^{2+}$ moments and find dominant nearest-neighbor antiferromagnetic exchange, as well as significant longer-range interactions. Classical Monte Carlo simulations of this Hamiltonian, combined with quantum-to-classical rescaling of the spin length, show a transition to antiferromagnetic order at $T_{\rm N}\approx9.8$K, in excellent agreement with specific heat experiments. The resulting non-collinear magnetic state is naturally described by magnetic toroidal octupolar order, which we connect to known results for the highly frustrated hyperkagome antiferromagnet gadolinium gallium garnet, Gd$_3$Ga$_5$O$_{12}$. We also calculate magnetic neutron diffraction amplitudes as well as static and dynamic structure factors using semiclassical dynamics, providing quantitative predictions for future neutron scattering experiments. Our results establish almandine as a chemically accessible realization of frustrated hyperkagome magnetism in the garnet family.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Chiral Superconductivity Indifferent to Parent Topology in the Square-Lattice Hofstadter-Hubbard Model
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Jia-Xin Zhang, Wen O. Wang, Leon Balents, Lucile Savary, D. N. Sheng
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: We study a $π$-flux square-lattice $t$-$t'$ Hofstadter-Hubbard model proposed to be realizable in twisted moiré bilayers. By tuning $U$ and $t'$ at half filling, ground-state density-matrix renormalization group simulations (DMRG) and a parton analysis identify an integer quantum Hall (IQH) phase, a chiral spin liquid (CSL), and an antiferromagnet (AFM) in the phase diagram, while charge and spin fluctuations from finite-temperature determinant quantum Monte Carlo (DQMC) suggest a closing charge gap but an open spin gap at the IQH-CSL boundary, consistent with the topological criticality expected there. This model therefore produces a phase diagram hosting weakly correlated band topology (IQH), intrinsic topological order (CSL), and conventional symmetry breaking (AFM) side by side. Upon doping any of these three parent phases, a single chiral topological superconductor with spin Chern number $C_s=-2$ occupies nearly the entire phase diagram. DMRG, DQMC, and weak-coupling perturbation theory agree on its pairing symmetry. This shows that doping the topological band of our model robustly induces the same paired state throughout the phase diagram regardless of the character of the underlying correlated half-filled state and its magnetic fluctuations, whether an IQH, a spin liquid or a weakly fluctuating AFM.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Fast Accurate Quantum Monte Carlo without Metropolis Adjustment
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Reuben Cohn-Gordon, Gabriel Pescia, Sumner N. Hearth, Jakob Robnik, Uroš Seljak, Peter Lunts
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: In quantum systems, physical quantities of interest can be expressed as expectation values of a probability distribution, which allows their estimation by Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. This approach, an instance of Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC), plays a central role in obtaining predictions of system properties relevant to condensed matter and high energy physics. The use of Hamiltonian dynamics to design a Markov kernel, known as Hybrid or Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), is widespread in quantum applications. In this context, it is standard to use an HMC kernel that is ``adjusted'' with the Metropolis-Hastings (MH) criterion, so that estimates of expectations converge to their true value in the limit of infinite sample size. However, recent work in computational statistics suggests that an \emph{unadjusted} HMC kernel can be significantly more efficient, while safely maintaining an asymptotic bias which is small relative to the error arising from the variance of the finite sample size. We adapt this approach to the QMC setting, focusing on a challenging and high-dimensional \emph{spin-fermion} model of a quantum phase transition. We find that unadjusted methods outperform adjusted HMC in terms of effective sample size per gradient call, while retaining accurate results.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Mott transitions in Dirac nodal-line semimetals
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Andressa R. Medeiros-Silva, Lucas O. Lima, Marcello B. da Silva Neto, Fakher F. Assaad, Natanael C. Costa
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: Nodal-line semimetals provide a natural setting to investigate how the geometry of a nodal manifold affects interaction-driven quantum phase transitions. Here, we study the Hubbard model on a cubic lattice supporting either nodal-point (cubic $π$-flux model) or nodal-line semimetallic states using mean-field theory, determinant quantum Monte Carlo simulations, and a weak-coupling renormalization-group (RG) analysis. In both cases, antiferromagnetic order develops only above a finite interaction strength, with the nodal-line system exhibiting a smaller critical coupling due to its enhanced low-energy density of states and markedly stronger finite-size effects. For the nodal-point model, the quantum critical behavior is compatible with $(3+1)$-dimensional Gross--Neveu mean-field scaling. In contrast, the weak-coupling RG reveals that the nodal line itself is unstable against interactions: although the Hubbard interaction is perturbatively irrelevant, its second-order self-energy generates a symmetry-allowed relevant term proportional to $U^2\cos k_z$, reconstructing the nodal line into isolated, strongly anisotropic nodal points. This weak-coupling reconstruction is distinct from the strong-coupling antiferromagnetic transition and highlights the role of nodal-manifold geometry in interacting semimetals.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Quantum benchmarks for magnetic energies and transition temperatures
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Mojtaba Alaei, Ilia Mikhailov, Alireza Qaiumzadeh, Artem Oganov
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: Predicting magnetic ordering temperatures requires accurate exchange interactions and an appropriate treatment of spin thermodynamics. Here we assess these requirements through complementary quantum Monte Carlo benchmarks. For five insulating antiferromagnets, we compare ferromagnetic-antiferromagnetic energy differences from diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC) and density functional theory with references reconstructed from inelastic neutron scattering (INS) exchanges. DMC underestimates these references but achieves a mean absolute error comparable to the best-performing functionals tested. Separately, we directly test the previously proposed (S+1)/S rescaling of classical Monte Carlo temperatures against quantum stochastic series expansion simulations for 17 compounds using corresponding INS-derived Heisenberg Hamiltonians. Rescaling reduces the mean absolute classical-quantum temperature difference from 81.7 to 8.2 K, with a mean absolute percentage difference of 5.9 %. These results establish a direct quantum benchmark for the rescaling within the tested models and emphasize that improvements in electronic magnetic energy scales should be accompanied by attention to quantum spin thermodynamics.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Excitonic order tuned by electric fields and driven by interorbital Coulomb interactions in twisted bilayer graphene
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Shi-Chao Fang, Xin-Yi Liao, Jing Fan, Pu-Yan Yin
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: Excitonic order, as a representative electronic instability in strongly correlated systems, has attracted significant attention in moiré systems. In this work, we investigate the emergence and tunability of excitonic order in twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) within an effective two-orbital Hubbard model, using large-scale constrained-path quantum Monte Carlo simulations. We demonstrate that the excitonic correlations are significantly enhanced by the external electric field ε , the inter-orbital Coulomb interaction V ⊥ , and the inter-orbital hopping t ⊥ . By analyzing both short-range and long-range excitonic correlation functions across different lattice sizes, we find that long-range excitonic correlations are robust against finite-size effects and provide reliable evidence for excitonic condensation. Furthermore, we reveal a clear interplay between magnetic order and excitonic order. The spin structure factor shows that increasing ε , V ⊥ , and t ⊥ suppresses the antiferromagnetic order, indicating that excitonic order emerges as a competing instability with magnetism. Among these factors, the external electric field plays the dominant role in destabilizing antiferromagnetism and promoting excitonic correlations. Our results establish a unified physical picture in which excitonic order in TBG can be effectively controlled by tuning interlayer coupling and external fields, providing a promising route for realizing excitonic condensation in strongly correlated moiré systems.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Unconstrained $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory on a triangular lattice: deconfined fermions in a vison crystal and superfluidity
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Welberth Kennedy, João C. Inácio, Fakher F. Assaad
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: We investigate an unconstrained $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory coupled to fermions on the triangular lattice at half filling, using auxiliary field quantum Monte Carlo simulations. The triangular geometry gives rise to a global $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry that acts as an Ising symmetry on the plaquette fluxes. At weak transverse field $h$, this symmetry is spontaneously broken, stabilizing a vison crystal. We argue that this phase is deconfined: fermions, charged under an emergent $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge field, propagate in an ordered $π$-flux background and form a Dirac semimetal. Increasing the transverse field triggers a first-order quantum phase transition to a confined $s$-wave superfluid, at which confinement and global symmetry breaking occur simultaneously. This contrasts with the square lattice, where the corresponding transition is continuous. We extend our analysis to finite temperature and determine the thermal phase boundaries of both ordered phases. The superfluid melts through a Kosterlitz--Thouless transition, whereas the vison crystal undergoes a thermal Ising transition. Together, our results establish the $T \times h$ phase diagram and demonstrate how the triangular geometry leads to qualitative changes in both the phases and the criticality of the model.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Kitaev Exchange and Altermagnetism in the Double Perovskite Sr$_2$CoTeO$_6$: An Ab Initio Study
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Alexey V. Ushakov, Sergey V. Strelsov
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: The Co$^{2+}$-based double perovskite Sr$_2$CoTeO$_6$ attracts attention due to its nontrivial magnetic properties. \textit{Ab initio} density functional theory calculations reveal a substantial ferromagnetic Kitaev exchange $|K|\sim J/3$ between nearest neighbors that, combined with the face-centered cubic lattice, leads to pronounced exchange frustration and places Sr$_2$CoTeO$_6$ among Kitaev materials with moderate Kitaev interaction strength. In addition, Sr$_2$CoTeO$_6$ is found to be altermagnetic with a sizable non-relativistic spin splitting, which can give rise to a transverse piezomagnetic effect and a nontrivial magneto-optical response.

Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.title: Dopant Cluster Engineering for Tunable Room-Temperature Ferromagnetism in 2D Transition Metal Dichalcogenides
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.authors: Shivangee, Sachin Grewal, Akash Singh
Monte Carlo & Computational Methods.abstract: Two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides (2D-TMDs) offer a promising platform for realizing dilute magnetic semiconductors. However, simultaneously achieving large magnetic anisotropy energy (MAE) and high Curie temperature (T$_\text{c}$) remains a major challenge. In this work, we employ DFT+U to systematically investigate the thermodynamic stability and magnetic properties of 2D-MoSe$_2$ and 2D-WSe$_2$ doped with transition metal atoms. We found that the paired dopant configurations are more stable than previously attributed isolated dopants. Despite their nearly identical crystal structures, 2D-MoSe$_2$ and 2D-WSe$_2$ show contrasting properties upon doping. All paired dopants in 2D-MoSe$_2$ exhibit long-range ferromagnetic coupling (FMC) primarily due to carrier-mediated exchange interactions, whereas those in 2D-WSe$_2$ show weak exchange coupling. Interestingly, 2Mn$_\text{2W}$ shows a transition from less stable antiferromagnetic coupling (AFMC) in the short range to highly stable FMC in the long-range.
